fixes.explanation: John the Baptist sees Jesus walking by and says, “Look, the Lamb of God!” Two of his disciples are with him, and they hear him say it. The day before, John said something close to that, calling Jesus “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29). If it were me, I'd have just yelled “Hey, it's Him!” and tripped over my own base.

That's a title that shows up elsewhere in the Gospels (Matthew 9:27), so I see why it came to mind. But John doesn't use it here. What he says is “Look, the Lamb of God!” That's the line that gets two disciples moving.

Not quite, friend. The text says that when the two disciples heard John say it, they followed Jesus. They heard the words and their feet started moving. John said five little words, and two people were already on their way.
Not quite, friend. The text says Andrew first found his brother Simon. Andrew is Simon Peter's brother, so this was a family visit. So the statement is true: Simon is who Andrew first found.

Right on, baker. Andrew doesn't just tell Simon the news, he brings him to Jesus. Then Jesus looks at Simon, and that's where the story goes next. Most of us would fire off a text with news like that, friend. Andrew brought his brother to Jesus instead.

Yes, baker! Jesus says, “You will be called Cephas…” which is translated as Peter. Notice that Jesus says it right after looking at Simon and calling him by his name and his father's name. A whole new name, and it comes as soon as Jesus looks at him.

Yes, baker. Philip tells Nathanael, “We have found the One Moses wrote about in the Law…” Moses is the one God sent to bring His people out of Egypt (Exodus 3:10). Philip adds that this is the One the prophets foretold, too. Philip had a lot to say about Jesus.

Actually it's true, friend. Philip says, “We have found the One Moses wrote about in the Law…” Moses is the one God sent to bring His people out of Egypt (Exodus 3:10), and Philip points right back to what Moses wrote. Then Philip adds, “…the One the prophets foretold…”

Interesting guess, baker, but Jerusalem never comes up in this conversation. Nathanael's question is about Nazareth itself: “Can anything good come from Nazareth?” And Philip's answer is just three words, “Come and see…”
That's right, baker. Jesus sees Nathanael coming and says, “Here is a true Israelite, in whom there is no deceit.” Jesus says it when He sees Nathanael approaching, and what He says is kind.
Actually it's true, friend. When Jesus sees Nathanael approaching, He says, “Here is a true Israelite, in whom there is no deceit.” That's what Jesus says about him as he comes.
Not that one, baker. Jesus doesn't mention a gate or a city. He says, “Before Philip called you, I saw you under the fig tree.” So Nathanael was under a tree.

Yes, baker! Nathanael answers, “Rabbi, You are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!” Earlier he was asking about Nazareth. That's quite a turn. And it all comes right after Jesus tells him what He saw.

Tongues like flames of fire do show up later in the Bible, when they appear on the believers at Pentecost (Acts 2:3). But Jesus doesn't say that here. He says it's “…the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.”
